The palette is a legend, not a grade. It is the wrong tool for green goggle work or for pale-leaf IR photography.
If lamps bloom and the room is grainy green, that is night vision. If foliage is white under a black sky, that is near-IR stills.
how: No key light in the usual sense. Contrast is delta-T.
Choose a palette and keep it consistent. Warm cores, cooler edges, possible bloom on the hottest spots.
Glass windows can block LWIR, so a face behind glass may fail. Prompt: thermal palette, heat as color, faces as warm masks, not green phosphor, not near-IR foliage.
when: A rider and horse as warm shapes on a cold ridge, ironbow or white-hot, breath as a plume, stone dark. Do not render it as a green night-vision feed or as daylight IR woods.
vs: Night Vision intensifies residual light on a phosphor. Infrared photographs near-IR reflectance (white leaves, dark sky).
Thermal is emitted LWIR. Monochrome is visible-light grey.
A thermal image can look mono in white-hot, but its tones follow heat, not albedo.
examples_film: Predator makes heat the alien's sight: bodies as warm figures in a cool jungle. Sicario uses thermal and related electro-optical views as raid and border seeing.
Those are device palettes, not looks to photocopy.
mistakes: Wrong cousin: night vision or near-IR photography. Tell: green grain with blooming streetlights, or white trees and black sky, or normal modeling from a key light.
Fix: temperature-based tones, warm bodies, cold surroundings, a named palette.

faq.q: What is thermal in film?
faq.a: An image of emitted heat mapped to a false-color or white-hot palette. It records temperature, not the light a normal camera would see.

faq.q: Thermal vs night vision
faq.a: Night vision amplifies light and usually looks green and grainy. Thermal paints heat. A cold dark room can still show a warm body on thermal.

faq.q: When should I use thermal?
faq.a: When the beat is temperature: hunting, rescue, targeting. Do not use it as a sci-fi grade on a normally lit scene.

faq.q: How do I prompt thermal for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the palette (ironbow, white-hot), say heat as color, warm faces, cool environment. Forbid green phosphor and near-IR foliage looks.

title: Transformation
narrative: A kiss turns the restaurant into a memory. A man becomes an animal in stages.
A liquid takes a face. Use it when the audience should not be allowed a cut to skip the becoming.

It is the wrong tool when you only need a landmark warp of one contour into another, or when a new scene should simply start. If the job is matched geometry between two portraits, morphing is cleaner.
If both body and world melt at random, the anchor is gone.
how: Decide what stays. A subject-stable world change matches pose, contact, and key while the background is exchanged by a move, an occlusion, a projection, a set change, or a tracked composite.
A body transformation stages makeup, puppet, or digital change in order, with weight and effort. Light the new state with a source that still makes sense on the skin.
Prompt a transformation of the subject: a body, room, or object becoming something else in continuous view.
when: Use it for the beat when becoming is the action: a memory room, a creature, a substance taking form. Do not use it as a morph between two unmatched stills.
vs: Morphing interpolates landmarks from one contour to another. Transformation can be practical, architectural, or a world swap around a stable person.
Morph uses the warp as an edit join. Creature stages (werewolf cinema) are performance and makeup, not only a warp.
examples_film: Vertigo 's revolving kiss shifts the surrounding setting toward memory. Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind lets memory spaces change around the couple.
An American Werewolf in London and The Fly stage the body as a visible change of state. Terminator 2 and The Abyss sit nearby as shape that reforms.
Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a generic morph of everything. The tell is melting faces and melting walls at once, no anchor.
The fix is a stable perceptual center and a designed change of state.

faq.q: What is transformation in film?
faq.a: Transformation makes a body, room, or object become something else in continuous view. The change is the scene, not a cut to a new state.

faq.q: Transformation vs morphing
faq.a: Morphing is geometric interpolation between matched forms. Transformation is a change of state that can be makeup, a walking set, or a world exchanged around a stable subject. One is landmarks. The other is becoming.

faq.q: When should I use transformation?
faq.a: Use it when the audience must watch the becoming: memory rooms, creature stages, a substance taking a face. Skip it for a simple fade or an unmatched morph.

faq.q: How do I prompt transformation for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Transformation of [Subject], a body, room, or object becoming something else in continuous view. Name the anchor and the new state. For video, transform across the shot.

title: Typography
narrative: A name walks the street. A credit is scratched into a notebook.
Type pursues a figure. Use it when the film should teach its pattern before or during the action, and when letters are part of the blocking.
It is the wrong tool for a lower-third, and a single handsome card is not yet a title sequence. If live action, drawing, and stock collide as equal media, you are in mixed media.
If paper layers tear without readable words as objects, you are in collage.
how: Choose one visual rule: ink that becomes a map, letters that stand in the set, type that tracks a body. Light in-world letters as surfaces (a key, an edge).
Reserve space for exact spelling. Animate progression before dropping credits.
The camera can dolly so type parallax against walls. Prompt typography in the world of the subject: words as objects, titles that occupy space, kinetic type.
when: Use it for the beat when a word must share space with a person, or when an opening must tell a miniature story in letters. Do not use it as unreadable scribble over a portrait.
vs: Mixed Media collides several capture modes. Typography can live inside a single photographed world.
Collage layers images. Type may appear there, but collage does not require words as blocking.
examples_film: Vertigo 's spiral opening sets a pattern of obsession in letter and shape. Se7en builds credits from hands, notebooks, and material type.
Catch Me If You Can condenses pursuit into animated letterforms. Annie Hall and Scott Pilgrim vs.
the World put sentences into the scene. Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a title card or a caption. The tell is unreadable AI lettering, or type glued to the frame with no space in the set.
The fix is exact words, a surface, and a rule that progresses.

faq.q: What is typography in film?
faq.a: Typography here is kinetic type in the world of the shot: words as objects, titles that occupy space. A sentence lives in the picture rather than as a caption.

faq.q: Typography vs mixed media
faq.a: Mixed media collides live action, drawing, type, and stock. Typography can be letters inside one photographed space. The letters are the event, not one of several crashing media.

faq.q: When should I use typography?
faq.a: Use it when words must occupy the scene or when an opening needs a miniature story in letters. Skip it for a simple name card or unreadable overlay.

faq.q: How do I prompt typography for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Typography in the world of [Subject], words as objects, kinetic type. Specify the exact words, the surface, and the light. Do not ask for decorative lettering you cannot read.

title: Vignette
narrative: The corners lose stop. Attention pools in the center without a spotlight on the actor.
Vintage wide glass and some anamorphics do this unasked. Cameo lighting can look similar, but that is a lighting plot, not falloff in the optic.
Use it to hold the eye in, to mimic old glass, or to admit that the field is darker off axis. Keep it gentle enough that the sides still exist.

It is the wrong tool as a heavy post oval crushed onto every wide. If the edges go to black like a spotlight and the falloff is a perfect geometric shape unrelated to the lens, you have a filter, not an optic.
how: Wide-open vintage glass, a wide angle on a small coverage circle, or an ND or grad at the edges. Cosine-fourth falloff is natural.
Mechanical vignetting is the barrel cutting the bundle. In a grade, darken corners with a soft, lens-shaped roll, not a hard oval.
Prompt: natural optical vignette, edges falling off, vintage falloff, not a post oval.
when: A rooftop figure at blue hour, corners a stop down, center holding the coat and the city. Do not crush the sides of a group shot until the people at the edge disappear.
vs: Cameo Lighting lights a figure against a dark field. The darkness is in the set, not in the glass.
Vintage Cine Glass often includes natural vignette plus aberrations. Central Framing is a compositional choice that vignette can support.
Halation glows highlights. Vignette darkens edges.
examples_film: Barry Lyndon shows fast vintage glass with natural corner falloff in candlelit rooms. The Witch uses older optics whose edges go quietly, holding the eye in the clearing or the kitchen.
mistakes: Wrong cousin: a circular crop, cameo spotlight, or a heavy social-media oval. Tell: perfect ellipse of black, subjects at the edge crushed, no relation to the lens.
Fix: soft, stop-based roll, keep edge information, match the glass.

faq.q: What is a vignette in film?
faq.a: Darkening or contrast loss at the frame edges from optics, the barrel, a filter, or a grade. Optical vignette is falloff. A post oval is an added shape.

faq.q: Vignette vs cameo lighting
faq.a: Cameo lighting is a dark set with a figure lit in the middle. A vignette is the frame itself losing light toward the corners, even if the set is even.

faq.q: When should I use a vignette?
faq.a: To hold the eye in or to match vintage glass. Do not crush the sides as a default filter, especially on groups and wides that need the edges.

faq.q: How do I prompt a vignette for AI image or video?
faq.a: Request natural optical falloff, a stop or so in the corners, and no hard post oval. Name vintage glass if that is the cause.

title: Wigglegram
narrative: A postcard comes alive as a cheap lenticular. The subject stays almost still.
The room jumps between two eyes. Use it when you want stereo without a move, a GIF of depth.
It is the wrong tool for a real tracking shot, and it is not camera shake. If planes peel continuously, you have parallax from travel.
If the same viewpoint chatters, you have a wiggle or a stutter.
how: Lock two (or three) stills on a stereo baseline of a few centimeters, same height, same lens. Flicker A-B-A.
Foreground shifts more than the back, which is the disparity. No motion blur from a pan.
Light both frames with the same key so only position changes. Prompt a wigglegram of the subject: two or three frames rocking, a cheap stereo shiver.
For video, a short wiggle between two viewpoints.
when: Use it for the beat that should feel like a lenticular or a stereo GIF: a portrait, a product, a joke of depth. Do not use it in place of a dolly through a room.
vs: Parallax comes from the camera traveling so planes peel at different speeds. A wigglegram only rocks between two locked viewpoints.
Stutter / Stop-Stutter is a temporal step of one take. Wiggle is a tiny tremor of the support, not a stereo pair.
examples_film: Lenticular photos and GIF stereo are the well-known uses: postcards, early web 3D fidgets, social stereo stills. Cinema borrows that twitch.
Grammar of two eyes, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousins are Wiggle shake and a mini Dolly In . The tell is blur from motion, or a continuous path.
The fix is two sharp stills a few centimeters apart, flickering.

faq.q: What is wigglegram in film?
faq.a: A wigglegram rocks two or three frames from slightly different viewpoints so depth reads as a stereo shiver. It is a fidget of disparity, not a camera move.

faq.q: Wigglegram vs parallax
faq.a: Parallax is continuous relative motion of planes as the camera travels. A wigglegram is a short loop between two locked stereo stills. One is a path. The other is a twitch.

faq.q: When should I use a wigglegram?
faq.a: Use it when depth should feel like a lenticular postcard or a stereo GIF. Skip it when the scene needs a real tracking shot.

faq.q: How do I prompt wigglegram for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Wigglegram of [Subject], two or three frames rocking, a cheap stereo shiver. For video, a short wiggle between two viewpoints. Keep the subject still and the baseline small.

title: X-Ray
narrative: Skin becomes a veil. The interior is the subject.
Use it when the story needs to see through: a medical look, a machine's vision, a suitcase, a chest. It is the wrong tool for heat, and for foliage that glows in near-infrared.
If warmth is false color, you want thermal. If leaves go pale and skies go dark, you want infrared.
how: Render or photograph as transmission: denser parts (bone, metal) hold more of the beam and read as structure. Invert or not, but keep a graphic interior with little surface makeup.
A hard, even backlight through the subject helps. Keep one body readable as a diagram, not a smear of glow.
Prompt an x-ray view of the subject: interior structure, bones or wiring, a body as diagram.
when: Use it for the beat of seeing through a person, a wall, or a device. Do not use it as a teal grade on ordinary skin.
vs: Thermal maps heat as false color. Infrared is near-IR reflectance, often odd foliage and skin, not a skeleton.
X-ray is transmission through the object, structure as diagram.
examples_film: The Abyss HUD and science films treat seeing-through as a device overlay or a laboratory plate. Superhero x-ray vision is the pop grammar of the same diagram.
Uses of interior structure, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousins are Thermal and a ghostly double exposure. The tell is heat colors, or a transparent person with a normal room and no structure.
The fix is bones or wiring as the picture, graphic, transmitted.

faq.q: What is x-ray in film?
faq.a: An x-ray look images through surfaces so interior structure, bones, or wiring become the picture. It is a diagram of density, not a photograph of skin.

faq.q: X-ray vs thermal
faq.a: Thermal shows heat. X-ray shows transmission through matter. One is temperature as color. The other is structure as a plate.

faq.q: When should I use x-ray?
faq.a: Use it when the story must see through a body, a wall, or a machine. Skip it for night hunts (thermal) or for IR foliage looks.

faq.q: How do I prompt x-ray for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write X-ray view of [Subject], interior structure, bones or wiring, a body as diagram. Specify transmission and a readable interior. Do not ask for heat colors.

title: Zoetrope
narrative: A horse's legs become a ring of stills. A spinning body is a drum of slices.
Use it when the point is that motion is made of frames, a toy of persistence of vision on screen. It is the wrong tool for ordinary slow motion, and for stop-motion of a puppet that never spins.
If you repeat frames of a continuous take to stutter time, that is step-printing. If an object is posed per frame on a table, that is stop-motion.
how: Strobe the action, or present discrete poses around a rotation, like slits in a drum. Each slice is sharp.
The gaps are the point. A hard, brief source (strobe, shuttered light) freezes each pose.
The camera can be locked on the drum or on a repeating run. Prompt a zoetrope of the subject: stroboscopic slices of a spinning action, motion as a drum of frames.
For video, stroboscopic zoetrope slices in repeating action.
when: Use it for the beat that should look like a Victorian motion toy, or a spin sampled into poses. Do not use it as a generic choppy grade on a walk that is not a drum of frames.
vs: Stop Motion poses an object once per frame. A zoetrope samples a spin or a repeating action as a ring of slices.
Step Printing repeats frames of a photographed take to slow or stutter it. The zoetrope shows the drum.
examples_film: The Horse in Motion is the scientific ancestor: sampled gait as a sequence of stills. Batman Begins uses zoetrope imagery as a motion toy inside the story.
Grammar of sampled spin, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousins are Slow Motion and Stutter / Stop-Stutter . The tell is a fluid overcrank, or a walk that hitch-steps without a drum of slices.
The fix is strobe-sharp poses around a repeating spin.

faq.q: What is zoetrope in film?
faq.a: A zoetrope treatment shows the frames inside a movement, like stroboscopic slices of a spinning action. Motion reads as a drum of poses.

faq.q: Zoetrope vs stop motion
faq.a: Stop-motion animates an object pose by pose. A zoetrope samples a spinning or repeating action as slits of frames. One is a puppet on a table. The other is a drum of slices.

faq.q: When should I use zoetrope?
faq.a: Use it when you want the audience to see sampling: a spin, a gait, a Victorian motion toy. Skip it as a random choppy look on ordinary coverage.

faq.q: How do I prompt zoetrope for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Zoetrope of [Subject], stroboscopic slices of a spinning action, motion as a drum of frames. For video, repeating strobe slices. Keep each pose sharp.

title: Choker Shot (BCU)
narrative: A choker traps a person in their own face. There is nowhere to gesture, no collar to hide in, no room tone in the corners.
Emotion has to happen in the eyes, the mouth, and the tiny muscles around them. It is the wrong tool when you still need a swallow, a shoulder, or a hand at the chest.

It is also the wrong tool if you only wanted pores on one feature: that job belongs to a tighter fragment. Hold a choker when the scene is a confession, a breakdown, or a stare with no escape, then cut out before the crop feels like a passport photo.
how: Put the top frame at the hairline and the bottom at the chin. Ears often clip.
Headroom is nearly zero. A 75mm to 100mm from portrait distance keeps the face from ballooning; a wide lens this close will warp the skull.
Camera at Eye Level unless you want a power tilt. Focus the nearer eye.
Light can be hard enough to show sweat, or wrapped if the performance is the only contrast. Prompt: Choker shot of [Subject] from hairline to chin, almost no background.
when: Use it when emotion has nowhere to hide: a whispered admission, a stare across a table that has become a cell. Do not use it if you still need upper body language, or if the story is actually one feature (an eye, a mouth) rather than the whole face.
vs: An Extreme Close-Up is tighter than the face: one feature, not hairline-to-chin. A Close-Up includes the upper shoulders and a little air around the head.
A choker, also called a big close-up or BCU, is the in-between prison: a complete face with no body. Do not treat BCU and ECU as synonyms.
examples_film: Persona pushes faces until they occupy the whole rectangle and start to trade identity. Black Swan uses this proximity when the performance has no backstage left.
Use those as grammar for pressure, not as a look-alike brief.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is an Extreme Close-Up (only an eye) or a Close-Up (shoulders still in). The tell is either a fragment with no chin, or a collar and headroom.
Fix: hairline and chin are the frame lines; nothing below the jaw.

faq.q: What is Choker Shot in film?
faq.a: A choker shot, also called a big close-up (BCU), is a very tight face crop, usually from hairline to chin, with almost no background and no shoulders. It is not an extreme close-up of a single feature.

faq.q: Choker Shot vs Close-Up
faq.a: A close-up holds the head and upper shoulders, so a little body and air remain. A choker cuts at the chin and hairline, so the face is the entire subject. If you can still see clavicle or coat collar, you are in close-up, not choker.

faq.q: When should I use Choker Shot?
faq.a: Use it when a face has nowhere to hide: confession, panic, a stare that is the scene. Do not use it for ordinary dialogue, and do not use it when the story is one feature rather than the whole face.

faq.q: How do I prompt Choker Shot for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Choker shot of [Subject] from hairline to chin, almost no background. Forbid shoulders. For video, keep that crop locked so a nod does not introduce chest or sky.

title: Close-Up (CU)
narrative: A close-up is a new fact on a face. It is the default for important dialogue because micro-expression, a lie, or a decision can be read without losing the idea of a person.
The shoulders keep a little body in the sentence so a swallow or a turned collar still exists. It is the wrong tool when the beat is a hand, a holster, or the door across the room.
It is also the wrong tool as a beauty setting on every line: if you live here, coverage becomes a slideshow of heads. Change size when the new scale reveals a fact this crop cannot prove.
how: Bottom frame at the upper chest or clavicle; top just above the hair, with modest Headroom . A 65mm to 85mm at conversation distance is common; the catalog 75mm Cooke is a portrait working length, not a requirement.
Shallow Focus will drop the room, but the size is the crop, not the bokeh. Match reverse size if this is dialogue.
Prompt: Tight close-up of [Subject], head and upper shoulders.
when: Use it to read micro-expression on an important line: the moment a person decides not to answer. Do not use it as wallpaper on every sentence, and do not use it when the information is below the chest.
vs: A Choker Shot cuts off the shoulders and sits on hairline and chin. A Medium Close-Up starts at the chest and still shows dialogue-distance body language.
An Extreme Close-Up is a fragment inside the face. Close-up is the portrait size: head plus upper shoulders, not MCU, not choker, not ECU.
examples_film: The Passion of Joan of Arc builds trial pressure from faces that still read as heads, not only fragments. The Silence of the Lambs uses close-ups in the interviews so thought is visible while a little of the body remains.
Grammar: the face as the location, with enough shoulder to stay a person.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Medium Close-Up (too much chest and room) or a Choker Shot (no shoulders). The tell is either a talking-head with a lot of torso, or a face with no neck.
Fix: head and upper shoulders only. Another tell is calling any tight face a close-up when you meant ECU.

faq.q: What is Close-Up in film?
faq.a: A close-up is a shot that frames a face or object tightly enough that detail outranks the surroundings, typically head and upper shoulders. It is a size, not a mood, and it still shows a person rather than one isolated feature.

faq.q: Close-Up vs Medium Close-Up
faq.a: A medium close-up starts at the chest and keeps shoulders and some hand language readable at dialogue distance. A close-up is tighter: head and upper shoulders, with the room mostly gone. If you can still see mid-chest and a slice of set, you are in MCU.

faq.q: When should I use Close-Up?
faq.a: Use it when an important line or thought must be read on the face. Do not park every line here, and do not use it when the beat is a hand, a door, or a whole-face prison crop.

faq.q: How do I prompt Close-Up for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Tight close-up of [Subject], head and upper shoulders. Add a 75mm if you want portrait proportion. For video, hold that crop; do not say close-up if you mean chest-up or hairline-to-chin.

title: Cowboy Shot
narrative: The cowboy exists because hands are plot. A gun, a bottle, a fist, a coat hem at the thigh: the stance is the sentence.
You get face and threat or ease in one frame without spending the extra air that feet and floor demand. It is the wrong tool when gait, shoes, or the full costume silhouette is the information.

It is also the wrong tool for table talk: you will be cropping a booth at mid-thigh for no reason. Use it for standing confrontation, weapons, and posture, then go tighter for the eyes or wider for the walk.
how: Bottom frame through mid-thigh. Holster, hanging hands, and coat edge should read.
A 35mm to 50mm from a few steps back is common. Pairing with Hip Level puts the lens near the gunbelt; that height is a choice, not the size itself.
You can shoot a cowboy at eye height. Prompt: Cowboy shot of [Subject] framed mid-thigh up, hands visible at the holster line.
when: Use it to show hands, weapons, or stance without going full body: a hand hovering at a belt, a bottle hanging, a ready posture. Do not use it if you need feet and walk, or if the beat is only a face.
vs: A Medium Shot cuts at the waist, so the holster and hanging hands are gone. A Full Body includes head to toe and a strip of floor.
Cowboy is the mid-thigh sentence: American shot, not MS, not full figure. Do not call it a medium long shot as if that erased the holster line.
examples_film: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly uses this standing size so guns and faces share one frame before the eyes take over. Django Unchained keeps hands and weapons readable in the same band.
Grammar: stance plus face, not a landscape and not a waist-up talk shot.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Medium Shot (waist) or a Full Body (feet in). The tell is a belt-only crop, or shoes.
Fix: bottom frame through the thigh, hands in, feet out. Another tell is a sitting medium labeled cowboy because the genre is Western.

faq.q: What is Cowboy Shot in film?
faq.a: A cowboy shot frames a person from mid-thigh or knees up so the hands remain visible at the holster line. It is also called an American shot. It is a standing size for stance and weapons, not a synonym for medium or full body.

faq.q: Cowboy Shot vs Full Body
faq.a: Full body includes the feet and a little floor; the whole figure is complete. A cowboy stops at mid-thigh, so gait and shoes are out while hands stay in. If you can see boots on the ground, you have left cowboy.

faq.q: When should I use Cowboy Shot?
faq.a: Use it when hands, weapons, or stance matter and you do not need the walk. Do not use it for table dialogue or for costume-and-gait beats that require feet.

faq.q: How do I prompt Cowboy Shot for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Cowboy shot of [Subject] framed mid-thigh up, hands visible at the holster line. Say American shot if that helps the model. Forbid feet and forbid a waist crop.

title: Cut-ins
narrative: The master already showed the table. The cut-in shows the text on the phone, the blood at the cuff, the grip on the glass.
Because the object was in the wider shot, the audience does not feel teleported. They feel informed.
It is the wrong tool when the detail was never in the geography (a sudden letter from nowhere) or when you leave the action for a clock on another wall. Those are insert-as-new-object and cutaway.
A cut-in is tighter, same world, same beat, often the same lens axis.
how: From the Master Shot or a wider size, punch in on a detail that was already visible, keeping screen direction and roughly the same camera axis. An Axial Cut is the hard version of this: a jump along the lens axis.
Match key side. Prompt: Cut-in on a detail of [Subject] already in the master, tighter, the same axis, a fact the wide cannot prove.
when: Use it to show the hands, the phone, the wound that the wide already contained but could not prove. Do not change axis so violently that it reads as a new setup, and do not cut in on an object that was not there.
vs: An Insert Shot may introduce a plot object in close view; a cut-in tightens on what the wide already had. A Cutaway leaves the primary action.
An Axial Cut is the editorial jump along the axis; cut-ins are the tighter shots you land on. An Extreme Close-Up may be the size of the cut-in, but ECU is the crop, not the coverage move.
examples_film: Classical coverage is built on this grammar: master, then cut in to the business that the master only implied. You see it whenever a wide conversation yields a closer pair of hands without leaving the table.
Use that as the rule, not as a specific poster frame.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Cutaway (you left) or an Insert Shot of a new object. The tell is a different wall, a new prop, or a reverse angle pretending to be a punch-in.
Fix: same space, same axis, tighter on a fact that was already there.

faq.q: What is Cut-ins in film?
faq.a: A cut-in is a closer shot of a detail that already exists in a wider view of the same space, often on the same axis. It shows the hands, the phone, or the wound the wide could not prove.

faq.q: Cut-ins vs Insert Shot
faq.a: An insert is a designed close view of a story detail, which may or may not have been readable in the master. A cut-in specifically tightens on something already in that wider shot. If the object appears from nowhere, you are inserting, not cutting in.

faq.q: When should I use Cut-ins?
faq.a: Use it when the wide has the geography and you need the small fact. Do not use it to leave the scene, and do not use it to introduce a prop that was not there.

faq.q: How do I prompt Cut-ins for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Cut-in on a detail of [Subject] already in the master, tighter, the same axis, and name the fact. Keep the same key and geography as the wide.

title: Cutaway
narrative: A cutaway is a brief exit: a clock, a kettle, a street, a person listening in a doorway. Its value is the relation it adds, not merely that it hides a bad join.
It can build anticipation, let the room comment, or imply that time has passed. It is the wrong tool when the object is the plot in the actor's hands: that is an insert.
It is also the wrong tool if the return to the main action restarts a gesture that should have continued. Check temporal logic.
A cutaway can be a pressure release; it can also cheat geography if the new view could not exist at that moment.
how: Choose a detail that can plausibly be present now. Match ambient light and, in editorial thinking, room sound.

Return to the main action at a later phase of the motion, not at the same frame of a handshake. Prompt: Cutaway from [Subject] to a related detail in the same world, a pressure-release or information beat that is not an insert on the actor.
when: Use it to hide a cut, show a clock, or let the room comment: a kettle trembling during an argument, a courtyard while someone looks. Do not cut away to a new geography that implies false time, and do not call an object-in-hand a cutaway.
vs: An Insert Shot stays on a plot object inside the action. A Reaction Shot is a person's response, often a face; a cutaway might be that listener, or it might be a non-human detail.
A cut-in goes tighter on something already in the master, same space and often same axis, without leaving the beat. Cutaway means you left.
examples_film: Hot Fuzz uses cutaways as both joke and glue. The Conversation lets the world around a listener comment.
Dancer in the Dark brackets a car conversation with wider and closer views. Jurassic Park punctuates approaching threat with environmental details and observers.
Grammar: leave, add a relation, return honestly.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is an Insert Shot (object in the action) or a random pretty detail. The tell is a letter in the hero's hands labeled cutaway, or a return that rewinds the action.
Fix: leave the primary beat, pick a plausible now, watch time on the way back.

faq.q: What is Cutaway in film?
faq.a: A cutaway is a shot away from the primary action, used for context, reaction, compression, or continuity repair. It might be a clock, a street, an observer, or a piece of the room.

faq.q: Cutaway vs Insert Shot
faq.a: An insert is a close view of a story object or hand fact inside the action. A cutaway leaves that action for a related view. Hands on the plot letter are an insert; the kettle on the stove during the fight is a cutaway.

faq.q: When should I use Cutaway?
faq.a: Use it to add a relation, hide a join, compress time, or let the world comment. Do not use it to show the object in the actor's hands, and do not return in a way that rewinds the action.

faq.q: How do I prompt Cutaway for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Cutaway from [Subject] to a related detail in the same world, and name that detail. Say it is not an insert on the actor. Match light to the main scene.

title: Establishing Shot
narrative: Before coverage begins, or when a scene has drifted, the audience needs to know where and when. An establishing shot declares the building, the street, the hour, the weather, sometimes the class of the place.
A later re-establishing shot can remind us of the same geography after the scene has moved. It is the wrong tool when you actually needed the skeleton of the action: that is a master.
It is also the wrong tool as empty postcard filler. Not every empty room is a pillow shot; placement and duration create the function.
A clock, a sign, or a doorway can establish. A huge landscape that never connects to the next cut does not.
how: Choose a vantage that names spatial relations: who can reach which door, which way is the city, what the light is doing. Often a Wide Shot or Extreme Long Shot , sometimes a facade, an aerial, or an unpeopled interval.
Hold long enough to read time of day. Preserve ambient sound in editorial thinking even if you are prompting a still.
Prompt: Wide establishing shot of [Subject] and the location at once, time of day and spatial relations declared before coverage begins.
when: Use it to open a scene or to tell us where and when: a hotel at blue hour, a jury building in morning smog, a re-establish after a time jump. Do not fire one on every recut if geography has not changed, and do not confuse it with a master that must play the scene.
vs: A Master Shot covers the dramatic action and blocking of this scene. An establishing shot names the place and time; it does not have to contain the argument.
An Extreme Long Shot is a size that often does this job. A Wide Shot is environment-forward coverage inside a scene, not automatically an establish.
A Long Shot places a person in land; that may or may not be the first image of the location.
examples_film: Blade Runner opens on a city that is already a time and a social order. The Shining uses the Overlook approach as geography before the interiors take over.
Tokyo Story and Late Spring let empty rooms and streets punctuate, which is related grammar: the world persisting between people. Peking Opera Blues reestablishes a party in broader views.
Use those as where-and-when grammar, not as frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Master Shot (action skeleton) or a pretty Extreme Long Shot with no relation to the next cut. The tell is a landscape postcard, or a wide that already plays the whole scene and gets labeled establish.
Fix: the shot should answer where and when, then coverage can begin.

faq.q: What is Establishing Shot in film?
faq.a: An establishing shot introduces or re-establishes location, geography, time, or social context. It is a function in the edit. It is often wide, but a sign, a clock, or a building can do the same job.

faq.q: Establishing Shot vs Master Shot
faq.a: A master covers the complete dramatic action and spatial blocking so you could play the scene in that one setup. An establishing shot tells you where and when, and does not have to contain the argument. You can cut from an establish into a master, or skip one if geography is already known.

faq.q: When should I use Establishing Shot?
faq.a: Use it to open a scene or to re-establish after a jump in time or place. Do not insert one as decoration on every reverse, and do not use it when you actually needed the scene's action covered in a master.

faq.q: How do I prompt Establishing Shot for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Wide establishing shot of [Subject] and the location at once, and name time of day and spatial relations. Put the place in the sentence, not only the person. Keep the next coverage in mind so the geography matches.

title: Extreme Close-Up (ECU)
narrative: Size is a sentence. An extreme close-up says the scene is this fragment: a pupil tightening, a lip splitting, a safety clicking off.

Cutting between such fragments can turn looking into a physical confrontation, as in a standoff built from eyes instead of bodies. It is the wrong tool when the actor still needs a whole face to play the line.
If you can still see hairline and chin together, you have not arrived at this size. Use it when a detail is the event, then get out before the texture becomes a poster.
how: Pick the anatomical landmark that hits the frame lines. Camera distance and focal length are separate from the crop: a 75mm or 100mm a few feet back keeps facial proportion; a wide lens inches from the skin balloons the nose.
A macro is only required when the feature is truly small, such as an iris or a watch gear. Tight framing, macro optics, and shallow depth of field are three different choices.
Light a small source if you want pore and scar; wrap if you want the fragment to stay readable. Prompt the exact feature and the crop (brow to upper cheek, mouth only), not a vague tight close-up.
when: Use it when a detail is the scene: the eye that decides to fire, the mouth that will not speak. Do not use it as a default portrait or for ordinary dialogue; the rest of the person is information you have thrown away.
vs: A Choker Shot still holds a whole face from hairline to chin. A Close-Up keeps head and upper shoulders.
An extreme close-up is a fragment, not a portrait. An Insert Shot can be this tight, but an insert is a story object or hand fact, not a size.
If the frame still includes both eyes and a mouth as a face, you are not here yet.
examples_film: In The Good, the Bad and the Ugly , eyes and faces dominate the final standoff montage until looking becomes the gunfight. The Passion of Joan of Arc puts interrogation pressure on facial fragments.
Persona uses faces so close that identity starts to fuse. Borrow the grammar of fragment versus whole, not a poster of an iris.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Choker Shot or a Close-Up : the whole face still reads. The tell is hairline and chin both present, or shoulders sneaking in.
The other tell is wide-angle distortion from parking a short lens on the nose. Fix: name the feature, crop inside the face, and pick a longer lens or a true macro only if the object is small.

faq.q: What is Extreme Close-Up in film?
faq.a: An extreme close-up is a shot size that fills the frame with one small feature such as an eye, a mouth, or a fingertip. It is tighter than a whole-face crop, so surrounding space becomes secondary or disappears.

faq.q: Extreme Close-Up vs Choker Shot
faq.a: A choker still shows a complete face from hairline to chin. An extreme close-up is a fragment: one feature, not the whole portrait. If both eyes and the mouth read as a face, you are in choker or close-up territory.

faq.q: When should I use Extreme Close-Up?
faq.a: Use it when the detail is the event: a trigger, an eye, a cracked lip. Skip it for ordinary talk, beauty portraits, or any beat that still needs the rest of the head and shoulders.

faq.q: How do I prompt Extreme Close-Up for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Extreme close-up of [Subject], name the single feature, and say it fills the frame tighter than forehead-to-chin. Add pores and texture if you need skin fact. For video, lock off and allow only a tiny motion in that feature.

title: Extreme Long Shot (ELS)
narrative: An ELS turns size into the emotion: awe, insignificance, loneliness, ambition. The small anchor lets the audience measure a space that would otherwise be abstract.
The land, the station, the spillway, or the void is the subject. It is the wrong tool when you still need a face, a costume, or even a clearly posed full figure.

It is also the wrong tool without a readable reference: huge architecture with no human, vehicle, or known object can look like a miniature. Use it when scale is the point, then come in when a person must act.
how: Keep the scale reference detectable through contrast, motion, or placement. Deep focus so terrain layers read; without depth cues the space flattens into a model.

An Aerial Pullback can arrive here by moving; the size itself can be a lock-off from a ridge or a high vantage. Prompt: Extreme long shot of [Subject] as a speck against vast terrain, landscape as the true subject.
when: Use it when scale is the emotion: a yellow coat at the base of a spillway, a rider swallowed by desert, a craft against a planet. Do not omit a readable reference object, and do not use it to cover dialogue.
vs: A Long Shot still presents a locatable full figure in large geography. A Wide Shot lets place speak inside coverage; bodies are small but not necessarily specks.
An Establishing Shot is a function that often uses this size but can also be a sign or a building. ELS is speck-scale.
Aerial Pullback is a move that can end on this size.
examples_film: Lawrence of Arabia lets figures and riders occupy vast desert until they are marks in sand. 2001: A Space Odyssey sets small human or spacecraft elements against immense environments.
Nomadland uses wide country the same way: the van and the body as scale, the land as subject. Grammar: measure the world, do not portrait the person.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Long Shot (person still a clear figure) or an Establishing Shot that is really a building postcard with no scale. The tell is a readable full-body pose, or a vast space that looks like a tabletop.
Fix: shrink the human to a mark, keep them findable, add depth cues.

faq.q: What is Extreme Long Shot in film?
faq.a: An extreme long shot makes environment and scale the subject, with any person reduced to a small reference in a much larger landscape or structure. Individual facial detail is gone on purpose.

faq.q: Extreme Long Shot vs Long Shot
faq.a: A long shot still shows a full, locatable figure in large geography. An extreme long shot makes that figure a speck and hands the frame to terrain, architecture, or sky. If you can costume-read the person, you are probably still in long shot.

faq.q: When should I use Extreme Long Shot?
faq.a: Use it when scale is the emotion and you have a readable human or object as a measuring stick. Do not use it for talk, and do not shoot empty vastness with no reference.

faq.q: How do I prompt Extreme Long Shot for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Extreme long shot of [Subject] as a speck against vast terrain, landscape as the true subject. Keep the scale reference detectable. Ask for deep focus and environmental depth cues so it does not look like a miniature.

title: Full Body (WS)
narrative: Full body is for costume, blocking, and gait. You need the shoes, the hem, the way weight sits on a hip, the path to the door.
The figure occupies most of the frame height, so this is a portrait of a body in space, not a map of a valley. It is the wrong tool when land must dwarf the person, or when the beat is a face.
Calling every complete figure a long shot or a wide shot erases this size. If the human is still large in the rectangle and the feet are in, you are here.
If they have become a small mark in weather, you have gone longer.
how: Keep head and feet both in, with a little floor and a little air. The figure should own most of the vertical.
A 35mm to 50mm from enough distance avoids stretching the legs; a 24mm too close will cartoon the feet. Do not confuse this with a 24mm Wide room map.
Prompt: Full-body shot of [Subject], head to toe, figure complete in frame, environment readable around the silhouette.
when: Use it when costume, blocking, and gait matter: a walk in a new coat, a stand in a doorway, a body that has to be seen whole. Do not use it when the land must win, or when you only needed mid-thigh for the hands.
vs: A Cowboy Shot stops at mid-thigh; feet are out. A Long Shot shows a full figure plus so much geography that the person is small in the world.
A Wide Shot lets place speak; bodies may be smaller still. Full body is the complete figure as subject, not cowboy, not long, not wide.
An Extreme Long Shot makes them a speck.
examples_film: The Searchers uses complete figures in doorways and desert edges so costume and stance read before the land fully claims them. Drive holds night walks head to toe so gait and scorpion jacket are the sentence.
Grammar: person complete, place as margin.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Long Shot (person small in land) or a Cowboy Shot (no feet). The tell is a tiny figure in weather, or a crop at the knee.
Fix: feet in, head in, person still large in the frame. Do not label it WS or LS just because the body is complete.

faq.q: What is Full Body in film?
faq.a: A full body shot shows a person head to toe, with the figure complete and some environment around the silhouette. The human remains the subject. It is not the same as a long shot or a wide shot, even if those names get used loosely.

faq.q: Full Body vs Long Shot
faq.a: In a full body shot the person fills most of the height; place is a readable border. In a long shot the full figure sits in substantial geography and could be ignored by the world. If the human is small in the rectangle, you have left full body.

faq.q: When should I use Full Body?
faq.a: Use it for costume, blocking, and gait. Do not use it when scale or landscape should dominate, and do not use it when hands-at-holster would have been enough.

faq.q: How do I prompt Full Body for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Full-body shot of [Subject], head to toe, figure complete in frame, environment readable around the silhouette. Forbid a speck-in-landscape result. Keep feet visible.

title: Gesture
narrative: Sometimes the scene is not the face and not the prop, but the almost-touch, the glove tightening, the look that does not land. Gesture coverage treats that small action as the beat.
Duration matters: the movement has a start, a peak, and a settle. It is the wrong tool when the object is the fact (a key, a letter) rather than what the body does.
It is also the wrong tool as a wide master where fingers die in the noise of a room. Get close enough that the motion reads, then let it finish.
how: Frame for the moving part. Hands often want a close crop without becoming a product shot; a glance may live in a Close-Up of the eyes.
Keep the body connected enough that the motion has a source (wrist, shoulder). Light to separate fingers from background.
Prompt: Gesture close on [Subject], the meaning in a hand, a glance, a weight shift, coverage of the small action.
when: Use it when the plot is in the fingers: an almost-touch in a corridor, a glove, a glass that does not quite rise. Do not cover it so wide the motion dies, and do not freeze it into an object insert.
vs: An Insert Shot is usually the object as fact. A Close-Up is a size that may hold a gesture, or may hold a still face.
An Extreme Close-Up can be a fingertip as texture rather than as action. Gesture means the expressive movement is the subject.
If nothing moves, you probably wanted an insert.
examples_film: In the Mood for Love builds withheld romance out of hands, glances, and slow weight shifts more than out of speeches. Drive lets gloves, a wheel, and small body decisions carry threat.
Grammar: the small action is the line.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is an Insert Shot of a still object, or a Close-Up of a face that never moves. The tell is a static prop hero, or a wide where the hand is a blur.
Fix: size to the moving part, let the action complete.

faq.q: What is Gesture in film?
faq.a: Gesture coverage is a shot sized and timed for a discrete expressive body movement: a hand, a glance, a shift of weight. The meaning is the action, not a still object and not a wide master of the room.

faq.q: Gesture vs Insert Shot
faq.a: An insert shows a story object or detail, often still enough to read as a fact. Gesture shows what a body does with or without that object. A key in the palm can be an insert; the hesitation before the hand closes is gesture.

faq.q: When should I use Gesture?
faq.a: Use it when the beat is a small body action the wide cannot prove. Do not use it for a still product-like object, and do not bury the motion in a master.

faq.q: How do I prompt Gesture for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Gesture close on [Subject], and name the hand, glance, or weight shift. For video, describe one motion and a settle. Keep the camera still unless the technique is a move.

title: Group Shot
narrative: A group shot is not a crowd still. It is a unit: people who share a table, a job, a crime, a bloodline.

The audience should be able to rank them at a glance: who sits, who stands, who is brightest, who is at the edge. It is the wrong tool when the politics are only two or three principals, or when you needed a master of action rather than a portrait of the unit.
Lighting everyone the same makes a yearbook. Let one face own the key, or let depth split generations.
how: Stage in layers: seated foreground, standing mid, a doorway back. Who is highest, central, nearest, brightest.

A slightly wider lens (35mm to 50mm) holds the unit without turning them into ants; go longer if you want compression to stack them. Prompt: Group shot containing [Subject] among several figures, ensemble blocking, who owns the frame by position and light.
when: Use it for a family, a crew, a jury: the unit as the subject. Do not light every face equally if someone owns the room, and do not use a group shot when the beat has become a two-person fight.
vs: A Three-Shot is specifically three principals. A Master Shot covers the complete action; a group shot may be that master, or it may be a posed unit inside a larger scene.
A Two-Shot is a pair. Group means the ensemble is the relation, usually more than three, still small enough to read as people rather than a mob.
examples_film: The Godfather stages families and crews so rank is seating, light, and who gets the center. Parasite uses household groupings the same way: who serves, who sits, who stands in a doorway.
Grammar: the unit, ranked.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Three-Shot labeled group, or a Master Shot so wide the faces die. The tell is three people, or a mob with no rank.
Fix: a small ensemble, readable faces, one person owning position or key.

faq.q: What is Group Shot in film?
faq.a: A group shot frames a small ensemble as one relational unit so belonging and dominance read through blocking and light. It is more than a trio, still small enough that people remain individuals.

faq.q: Group Shot vs Three-Shot
faq.a: A three-shot is three principals and their triangle. A group shot is a larger unit: family, crew, jury. If you only have three named people, write three-shot. If the unit is the household or the crew, write group.

faq.q: When should I use Group Shot?
faq.a: Use it when the ensemble is the subject and rank should be visible. Do not use it for a pair or a trio, and do not flatten everyone with equal light.

faq.q: How do I prompt Group Shot for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Group shot containing [Subject] among several figures, ensemble blocking, who owns the frame by position and light. Give a head count and name the dominant body.

title: Insert Shot
narrative: An insert is not a pretty prop break. It is a fact the wider coverage cannot prove: the handwriting, the latch, the cup of water beginning to tremble, the key in a palm.
Hands should be human-sized. The object should cut with the same key as the scene.
It is the wrong tool when you are leaving the action for a clock on the wall or a listener in another room: that is a cutaway. It is also the wrong tool as a glowing product hero.
If the object's specific mechanism never pays off, you may only have a MacGuffin in the plot, but the insert still has to be a readable picture of a thing.
how: Size to the object. Match the scene's key side and color so the cut belongs.
Macro only if the detail is small; a letter can be a close crop on a 50mm. Keep hands at real scale, no giant fingers.
Prompt: Tight close-up of an object that carries the plot near [Subject]: a glass, a letter, a latch. Hands at real scale.
No glowing skin.
when: Use it to point at the thing that will matter later: a key, a letter, a latch, a trembling glass. Do not insert a decorative object that never returns, and do not light it like a catalog hero if it lives in a messy room.
vs: A Cutaway leaves the primary action for context, a clock, or an observer. An Extreme Close-Up is a size; an insert is a job and may be that tight.
A cut-in tightens on something already proven in the wider shot, often on the same axis. A Gesture covers a body movement rather than an object.
Product lighting treats the object as a commercial portrait , which is a different job.
examples_film: Rear Window uses optical details as plot facts. Zodiac lives in handwriting and paper.
Notorious makes a concealed key a crucial object. Jurassic Park lets water in a cup reveal an approaching vibration.
The Maltese Falcon and North by Northwest organize pursuit around objects; those are story engines, while the insert is the picture of the thing. Grammar: show the fact.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Cutaway (leaving the action) or a Product hero (catalog glamour). The tell is a clock in another room, or black-sweep reflections on a plot letter.
Fix: same scene, same light, object at real scale, story reason to look.

faq.q: What is Insert Shot in film?
faq.a: An insert shot is a close view of a story-relevant detail, object, hand action, screen, or text. It is coverage of a plot fact, usually cut into a wider scene, with hands and objects at real scale.

faq.q: Insert Shot vs Cutaway
faq.a: An insert stays on a detail that belongs to the primary action: the letter in the hands, the latch, the glass. A cutaway leaves that action for a related piece of the world, such as a clock, a street, or a listener. If you have left the actor's beat, you are probably in a cutaway.

faq.q: When should I use Insert Shot?
faq.a: Use it when a detail will matter and the wide cannot prove it. Do not use it as decoration, and do not use it when you meant to leave the scene for context.

faq.q: How do I prompt Insert Shot for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Tight close-up of an object that carries the plot near [Subject], name the object, and specify hands at real scale. Match the scene light. No catalog glow.

title: Interview
narrative: An interview frame is not merely an MCU. It is a social geometry: the subject speaks to a person beside the camera, look space opens toward that listener, and the audience sits in on an answered question.
Direct address into the lens is a different contract (confession, host, warning). It is the wrong tool when two fictional characters are in a scene together and you needed OTS or a two-shot.
It is also the wrong tool if the eyeline hits the glass and you did not mean to break the fourth wall. Keep the size stable; hunting around the face turns testimony into a music video.
how: Size usually Medium Close-Up or a loose Close-Up . Camera at Eye Level .
Eyeline a few degrees off lens, toward an implied interviewer. Give Look Space on the look side.
Motivated, simple key; catchlight in the eyes. Prompt: Interview frame of [Subject], talking-head distance, eyeline just off lens, a listener implied.
when: Use it when someone is answering a question we did not hear: documentary testimony, a fake-doc confession, a talking-head insert in a drama. Do not put the eyeline into the lens unless you mean direct address, and do not use this grammar for a two-person scene that should be OTS.
vs: A Medium Close-Up is only a crop; interview is the off-lens eyeline plus implied listener. Eye level is the height.
Over-the-Shoulder would show the questioner. A video portrait holds a face as a study, often without the Q&A contract.
Interview means testimony geometry.
examples_film: The Fog of War parks a speaker in this grammar so policy becomes a face answering questions. Many social-issue films borrow the same talking-head language (including The Social Dilemma's interview mode): stable size, off-lens eyeline, a listener we take on faith.
Grammar: someone is being asked.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a generic Medium Close-Up with eyes into the lens, or an Over-the-Shoulder Coverage of a scene. The tell is a host stare, or a second character in a fictional blocking.
Fix: off-lens eyeline, implied listener, stable talking-head size.

faq.q: What is Interview in film?
faq.a: Interview cinematography is a talking-head setup in which the subject answers an offscreen questioner. Size is stable, the eyeline sits just off the lens, and a listener is implied even if we never see them.

faq.q: Interview vs Medium Close-Up
faq.a: MCU is a chest-up crop that can be used for any dialogue. Interview is a setup: off-lens eyeline, look space toward a questioner, testimony as the job. You can shoot an MCU that is not an interview, and an interview that is slightly tighter or looser than MCU.

faq.q: When should I use Interview?
faq.a: Use it for testimony, documentary talking heads, or a drama that borrows that contract. Do not use it when two characters should share a scene in OTS, and do not aim the eyes at the lens unless you mean direct address.

faq.q: How do I prompt Interview for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Interview frame of [Subject], talking-head distance, eyeline just off lens, a listener implied. Add look space and eye-level. For video, hold the size; do not tour the room.

title: Long Shot (WS)
narrative: A long shot places a human in a world that could continue without them. You still recognize a body, a walk, a horse, but land, street, or weather takes most of the rectangle.
The sentence is person-in-world, not person-as-portrait. It is the wrong tool when you need the face, the holster, or a complete figure that still owns the height of the frame.
It is also the wrong tool when the person has become an unreadable speck: that is farther still. Use it to locate a body in a place, then go closer for the decision.
how: Keep a full figure readable, then add enough architecture or terrain that the person does not fill the height. Working from farther back with a 24mm to 35mm, or from a ridge with a longer lens, both can get you here; the crop is the size.
Deep enough focus that the place reads. Prompt: Long shot of [Subject] small in a large environment, full figure plus geography.
when: Use it to place a human in a world that could ignore them: a rider on a ridge, a coat on a platform, a body in a square. Do not use it to read an eyelid, and do not use it when you only needed head-to-toe as a portrait.
vs: A Full Body keeps the person large, head to toe, with place as a border. A Wide Shot is environment-forward coverage: place still speaks, often as the map of a scene.
An Extreme Long Shot turns the figure into a speck and gives the land the subject. Long shot is full figure plus geography, not those three.
An Establishing Shot is a job (where and when), which may use this size.
examples_film: Lawrence of Arabia sets riders in desert so the person is still a figure and the land is already huge. Seven Samurai plants bodies in village dirt and fields the same way.
Grammar: locatable human, large world, not a postage-stamp speck and not a costume portrait.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Full Body (person fills the height) or an Extreme Long Shot (speck). The tell is either a fashion lookbook figure or a landscape with no readable human.
Fix: full figure visible, world dominant, person still a person.

faq.q: What is Long Shot in film?
faq.a: A long shot shows a full subject and a substantial portion of the environment, so a person is small in a large place but still readable as a figure. It is a size, not automatically an establishing shot.

faq.q: Long Shot vs Wide Shot
faq.a: A long shot is the person-in-world size: full figure plus geography. A wide shot is environment-forward coverage whose job is to let place speak and not isolate yet. They overlap in the wild, but wide is a coverage attitude; long is the figure-plus-land sentence.

faq.q: When should I use Long Shot?
faq.a: Use it to locate a human in a place large enough to ignore them. Do not use it for faces, and do not use it when you wanted a full-body portrait or a speck-scale landscape.

faq.q: How do I prompt Long Shot for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Long shot of [Subject] small in a large environment, full figure plus geography. Keep the body identifiable. Do not say head-to-toe hero and do not say speck.

title: Master Shot
narrative: A master protects the scene. If every close-up dies, you still have who sat where, who could reach the door, and how the argument moved through the room.
It is usually wide enough for blocking, not so wide that faces and props stop meaning anything. It is the wrong tool when you only needed to name the building from outside: that is an establish.

It is also the wrong tool as a lifeless wide you never intend to use, parked for safety while all the acting happens in mismatched singles. A moving master can carry the whole beat if blocking and camera path are designed together.
how: Set a camera that sees all essential blocking: seats, door, table, the path out. Size is often a Wide Shot or a loose Two-Shot , but the job is coverage of the action, not a particular crop.
Keep faces and key props readable enough to cut. Mark the 180.
You can later cut in or go to singles. Prompt: Wide master of [Subject] with all blocking visible, the skeleton of the scene in one continuous frame, coverage can cut in later.
when: Use it to protect the scene: a jury room argument that could play in one take, a party whose crossings you must understand. Do not skip it and hope singles will invent geography, and do not treat an exterior postcard as a master.
vs: An Establishing Shot says where and when; a master says what happens in this space. A Wide Shot is a size.
A Two-Shot may be the master if two people and their blocking are the whole scene. A Group Shot shows an ensemble as a unit; it is a master only if the complete action plays inside it.
You can always go tighter. You cannot always invent a door that was never in the skeleton.
examples_film: 12 Angry Men keeps returning to roomy views that clarify the changing jury arrangement so singles have a map. Nashville builds scenes whose wider coverage holds crossings and music as one geography.
Grammar: the scene could play here.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is an Establishing Shot (place, no action) or a Wide Shot that crops out the door you will need. The tell is a pretty exterior, or a wide so empty that the scene cannot play.
Fix: every important path and body must be in, and the take must be able to run the beat.

faq.q: What is Master Shot in film?
faq.a: A master shot is a setup that covers the complete dramatic action and spatial geography of a scene. It is the skeleton of the scene, often wide, and you can cut in tighter coverage later.

faq.q: Master Shot vs Establishing Shot
faq.a: An establishing shot introduces location and time. A master covers the action inside the scene: who moves where, who can reach whom. A skyline cannot be your master if the argument happens in a kitchen.

faq.q: When should I use Master Shot?
faq.a: Use it to protect the scene so geography and blocking remain true. Do not confuse it with an exterior establish, and do not shoot a lifeless wide you never intended to play.

faq.q: How do I prompt Master Shot for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Wide master of [Subject] with all blocking visible, the skeleton of the scene in one continuous frame. Name furniture, doors, and positions. For video, play the whole beat in that frame.

title: Medium Close-Up (MCU)
narrative: An MCU is how people talk when you still care about body language. You get the thought on the face and the small shrug, the glass raised, the cigarette, without dropping to the waist.
Most interview and table coverage lives here because the room is a slice, not a map. It is the wrong tool when the holster, the gait, or the architecture is the information.
It is also the wrong tool when the line needs a true close-up fact: an MCU will keep offering shoulders and wallpaper. Use it to talk; leave it when the scene stops being a conversation.
how: Bottom frame at mid-chest or the sternum. Hands can enter if they rise.
50mm to 75mm at sit-down distance is typical; the catalog 65 to 75mm is a working band, not a brand. You should still see a strip of set behind the shoulders.
Headroom is normal, not crushed. Prompt: Medium close-up of [Subject] from chest up, shoulders and hands still readable.
when: Use it for dialogue that must keep body language: two people at a table, a phone call with a free hand. Do not use it when you need a waist-up gesture, a gunbelt, or a face with no chest left in frame.
vs: A Close-Up is head and upper shoulders, tighter than chest-up. A Medium Shot starts at the waist and balances gesture with face.
MCU is the band between them: chest up, talk without losing the shoulders. Do not write MCU when you mean CU, and do not call a waist shot a medium close-up.
examples_film: Heat uses this distance in the diner so two opponents can talk with shoulders and hands still in play before and between tighter singles. The Sopranos lives in MCU for talk that still needs a room sliver and a raised glass.
Grammar: conversation distance, not a beauty crop.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Close-Up (torso gone) or a Medium Shot (waist in). The tell is either a floating head or a belt buckle.
Fix: crop at the chest, keep a hand possible, keep a slice of room.

faq.q: What is Medium Close-Up in film?
faq.a: A medium close-up frames a person from the chest or shoulders up, at dialogue distance. You can still read shoulders and often a hand, while the face remains the primary information.

faq.q: Medium Close-Up vs Medium Shot
faq.a: A medium shot starts around the waist, so rest-position hands, a table, and a belt line are in. An MCU starts at the chest, so it is tighter talk coverage. If the belt is in, you have left MCU.

faq.q: When should I use Medium Close-Up?
faq.a: Use it when people talk and you still need body language without going waist-up. Do not use it for holster, gait, or a true facial fact that needs a close-up.

faq.q: How do I prompt Medium Close-Up for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Medium close-up of [Subject] from chest up, dialogue distance, shoulders and hands still readable. Name 65 to 75mm if you want that working length. Keep the chest line in the shot.
